title: Why dimensional analysis works: general classification of self-similarity based on scale-invariance
abstract: In this work, we formulate self-similarity from the perspective of scale invariance, where a self-similar form is understood as the transformation of a function into a form invariant under scale transformations. By applying this formulation to physical parameters, which consist of numerical values and units, it is demonstrated that dimensional analysis works for physical problems because scale invariance is partially shared between units and physical parameters. This naturally leads to the distinction between similarity of the first kind and similarity of the second kind according to whether the scale functions induced by units and those associated with physical parameters are equivalent or not. Self-similar solutions of the second kind can be further classified according to whether the power exponents of the similarity parameters include functions of dimensionless numbers. This leads to the conclusion that there are three kinds of self-similar solutions. The present work provides a unified framework for understanding dimensional analysis and a universal classification of self-similarity in physical problems.
summary: This work provides a deep theoretical framework showing that self-similarity arises from scale invariance. It unifies dimensional analysis by proving it works because physical units and parameters share underlying scaling symmetries. The paper classifies all such solutions into three types based on the mathematical structure of their associated scale functions.
main_problem: To develop a unified framework for understanding dimensional analysis by rigorously formulating self-similarity from the perspective of scale invariance.
main_result: The paper establishes that there are three distinct kinds of self-similar solutions (Type I, II A, and II B) based on how intrinsic scale functions relate to unit transformations. It proves that dimensional analysis works because it exploits the partial sharing of scale invariance between physical units and parameters.
method: The core method involves applying group theory concepts related to scale transformations ($\sigma$) to governing equations, comparing these mathematical invariances with those derived from physical units, and classifying the resulting solutions hierarchically.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to various physical models, including one-dimensional diffusion processes, viscoelastic impact dynamics, and modified groundwater flow problems governed by non-linear partial differential equations.
key_observables: Self-similar profiles ($\Phi$), data collapse plots, and the structure of similarity parameters ($\Pi, Z$).
important_parameters: Scale factors ($A$), power exponents ($\alpha_{ik}$), dimensionless numbers (e.g., $c$ in groundwater flow).
main_assumptions: The derivation assumes that scale functions derived from unit structures can be applied to physical parameters due to the indistinguishability of their numerical transformations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate data collapse for diffusion processes and show hierarchical relationships between different classes of similarity parameters (First Class $ightarrow$ Second Class).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining scale invariance, then applying it to specific PDEs (diffusion, groundwater flow) to derive initial similarity forms. It then develops a general mathematical framework comparing unit scaling vs. parameter scaling, leading to the final three-fold classification of self-similarity.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the rigorous mathematical machinery developed for classifying scale invariance and dimensional reduction is highly relevant to analyzing critical phenomena or asymptotic regimes in complex many-body statistical mechanics models.

A self-similar solution of the first kind is characterized by the absence of an intrinsic scale function ξ, whereas a self-similar solution of the second kind possesses an intrinsic scale function ξ. Self-similar solutions of the second kind can be further subdivided into Type A and Type B according to whether the exponents appearing in ξ are constant or depend on additional dimensionless parameters.
